chapter: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
title: Mel Williams, Decca's race-record man and Fritz Pollard's teammate
summary: Danny describes Mel Williams as an All-American football player who ran Decca's Black repertoire and withheld royalties.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yes, Mel Williams. He was an All-American. Him and Fritz Pollard were on the same team, one of them teams that ran over everybody in the Eastern League...what do you call that league...? The Ivy League.

Mel Williams. He was... You get them people who make their big reputation in national and international sports, they always can get good jobs, because the White boys that go to school with them... They keep the positions hereditary, and they always can get a job. So Fritz Pollard (I saw him on the air the other night; he's a very old man), he was a young cat who weighed about 175 pounds, but he was
swift as lightning on the football field, and he made All-American -- him and Mel Williams.

So Mel Williams has got the Black repertoire of Decca. He records everybody, Joe McCord, all them people out of Chicago. He lived in Chicago. And he even started the Race Records which they call on the catalogue, in the Decca catalogue. So they're looking for talent.
